subsection: 5. Case study: de Valera in America, June 1919–December 1920

notes.h: Case study: de Valera in America, background and causes
notes.b: Éamon de Valera went to America in June 1919 as President of Dáil Éireann, after escaping from prison in England, to win recognition for the Irish Republic.
points: De Valera was born in New York in 1882 to an Irish mother and a father from Spain and Cuba, and he was raised in County Limerick.
He commanded the Volunteer garrison at Boland’s Mill in Dublin during the 1916 Rising, and his death sentence was commuted to imprisonment.
He was arrested in May 1918 in the round-up that followed the so-called German Plot, and he was held in Lincoln Gaol in England.
He escaped from Lincoln Gaol on 3 February 1919, in an escape planned by Michael Collins’s organisation.
In April 1919 the Dáil elected him President of Dáil Éireann, the government of the self-declared Irish Republic.
His aims in America were to win US recognition of the Republic, to raise funds for the Dáil government, to influence the Paris Peace Conference, and to affect the 1920 presidential election.
President Woodrow Wilson did not press Britain on Irish self-determination at the Paris Peace Conference, which limited what the mission could achieve there.

notes.h: Case study: the arrival and the tour, 1919
notes.b: De Valera arrived in America in June 1919 and toured cities with large Irish populations, where he was greeted by crowds, receptions and parades.
points: He arrived in the United States in June 1919, and he began a long tour of the cities with the largest Irish communities.
His meetings in cities such as Boston, Chicago and New York drew large Irish-American audiences, who gave him receptions and donations.
Irish-American organisations and parishes arranged his meetings, and local branches raised money and sent subscriptions to Dublin.
His message was recognition of the Republic, support for the Dáil, and funds for the struggle in Ireland.
The reception was enthusiastic among Irish Americans, while the American government and most of the press treated the mission with caution.
British officials objected to his tour, which they regarded as propaganda against British rule in Ireland.

notes.h: Case study: funds and the Dáil bond drive
notes.b: The bond drive was meant to raise a large sum for the Dáil government, and the amount it raised remains disputed.
points: The Dáil loan was sold to Irish Americans as bonds in the Irish Republic, so that supporters could invest in the struggle for independence.
The bond drive used the networks of Irish-American organisations, parishes and clubs to reach donors in cities across the United States.
The sum raised fell short of the target that the Dáil set, and historians give different totals for what reached Dublin.
Disputes arose over who controlled the money, and Irish-American leaders disagreed with de Valera about how the funds should be spent.
The bond drive gave the Dáil government a financial base in the diaspora, which was used alongside money raised in Ireland.

notes.h: Case study: the conflict with Irish-American leaders
notes.b: De Valera’s mission divided Irish America, and his clash with Devoy and Judge Cohalan weakened the unity of the movement.
points: John Devoy and Judge Daniel Cohalan led the Friends of Irish Freedom, which had supported Irish independence since 1916.
They quarrelled with de Valera over the control of funds and of the American movement, and the conflict was carried out in the press.
Devoy and Cohalan saw de Valera as trying to take control of an organisation they had built, while de Valera wanted an organisation that answered to the Dáil.
The split reduced the unity of Irish America, and the Friends of Irish Freedom lost some of its supporters to de Valera’s followers.
The quarrel showed the difficulty of running a movement from America when the leaders in Ireland had their own priorities.

notes.h: Case study: the 1920 conventions and the presidential election
notes.b: In 1920 de Valera tried to win a commitment to recognition from both major American parties, and neither convention gave one.
points: The Republican National Convention met in Chicago in June 1920, and the Democratic National Convention met in San Francisco in July 1920.
De Valera approached delegates and party leaders at both conventions, seeking a plank recognising the Irish Republic.
Neither convention adopted recognition of the Irish Republic, and the question was left out of the platforms that went forward to the election.
The Republican candidate Warren G. Harding won the presidential election in November 1920, and his administration did not recognise the Republic.

notes.h: Case study: the Westminster Gazette interview and the AARIR
notes.b: De Valera’s public statements in early 1920 caused controversy, and the campaign for recognition was reorganised in November 1920.
points: In February 1920 de Valera gave an interview to the Westminster Gazette, in which he used Cuba’s position as an analogy for Ireland.
The comparison with Cuba caused controversy among some American supporters, who felt it weakened the appeal for recognition.
The American Association for the Recognition of the Irish Republic was founded in November 1920 as a new organisation for campaigning and lobbying for recognition.
The new association organised rallies and lobbied members of Congress for recognition of the Republic.

notes.h: Case study: events in Ireland while he was away
notes.b: While de Valera was in America, the Anglo-Irish War intensified, and the British government passed a Government of Ireland Act that divided the island.
points: The Soloheadbeg ambush on 21 January 1919 marked the start of the Anglo-Irish War, which lasted until 1921.
The British government banned the Dáil on 12 September 1919, and the Dáil’s ministers went underground.
Michael Collins, as Minister for Finance and director of IRA intelligence, ran much of the war in Ireland while de Valera was in America.
On 21 November 1920, known as Bloody Sunday, IRA gunmen killed British intelligence officers in Dublin, and British forces then fired on a crowd at Croke Park.
The Government of Ireland Act, passed in December 1920, created separate parliaments for Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland.
De Valera returned to Ireland in December 1920, when the Government of Ireland Act was being passed.

notes.b: The mission secured publicity and money for the Republic, but not the recognition its leaders wanted.
points: No American government recognised the Irish Republic during the mission or in the years that followed.
The mission raised money for the Dáil government, but the total is disputed and was below the target.
The mission raised the profile of the Irish Republic in American newspapers and at public meetings.
The split among Irish-American organisations weakened the Friends of Irish Freedom and led to new bodies, including the American Association for the Recognition of the Irish Republic.
De Valera’s absence left the Dáil government without its president at a time of war, and relations between him and Michael Collins were strained during the absence.

notes.h: Case study: significance and differing views
notes.b: Contemporaries and later historians have judged the mission differently, as a fundraising success, a propaganda triumph or a failure to win recognition.
points: Irish-American supporters praised the energy and the fundraising of the mission, and they saw it as a sign of the Republic’s international standing.
British officials and much of the British press regarded the mission as dangerous propaganda aimed at the American public.
Irish nationalists in Ireland differed on the mission’s priorities, and some argued that the time spent in America should have been spent at home.
Historians disagree on the outcome: some see the mission as successful propaganda and fundraising, while others see it as a failure because recognition was never won.
The mission was one of the first major efforts by the Irish Republic to win international recognition, and it shows the limits of diaspora politics.

notes.h: Assessment: success or failure in America
notes.b: Judgements on the mission turn on whether recognition, money or publicity is taken as the measure of success.
points: Achievement: the mission brought the Irish Republic’s case to large American audiences and raised money for the Dáil government.
Limit: the American government never recognised the Republic, and the Irish-American movement was divided by the mission.
Contemporary view: supporters called the mission a triumph, while the British government and its allies called it dangerous and divisive.
Later view: historians stress that the mission was a propaganda success but a diplomatic failure, because the recognition it sought was never granted.

keyTerms.definition: The bonds sold to Irish Americans in 1919 and 1920 to raise money for the Dáil government and the struggle for independence.
The formal acceptance by a foreign government of the Irish Republic as an independent state, which the Dáil sought from the United States.

An Irish-American organisation founded in 1916 and led by Judge Daniel Cohalan, which split with de Valera during his American mission.
The assembly of elected representatives that claimed to be the parliament of the Irish Republic from 1919.
The conflict of 1919 to 1921 between the IRA and British forces, which ran alongside de Valera’s American mission.
The Act passed in December 1920 that created separate parliaments for Northern and Southern Ireland.
